title: What is an UPSERT (insert-or-update in one atomic statement) — `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` (PostgreSQL), `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` (MySQL), or the SQL-standard `MERGE` — and why is it safer than a separate SELECT-then-INSERT/UPDATE (race condition under concurrency)?

s1_definition.profdef: An UPSERT is a single atomic statement that inserts a row if it does not already exist and updates it if it does. PostgreSQL expresses it as `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE`, MySQL as `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, and the SQL standard as `MERGE`. It is safer than the naive pattern of SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE because that pattern has a race condition: between the SELECT and the write, another transaction can insert the same key, causing either a duplicate-key error or a lost update. The UPSERT performs the check-and-write as one indivisible operation protected by the unique constraint, so concurrency cannot slip in between.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India keeps a daily-balance row per account. The naive way is: check if today's row exists; if not, insert it; if yes, update it. Under load two requests can both check at the same time, both see "no row," and both try to insert — one crashes with a duplicate key. An UPSERT is like telling the clerk "create today's row, or if it already exists just update it" in one breath, so two simultaneous requests cannot both think they are the first.
s1_definition.oneliner: An UPSERT inserts-or-updates in one atomic statement; it beats SELECT-then-write because the latter races between the check and the write.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An UPSERT is a single atomic statement that inserts a row if it does not already exist and updates it if it does. PostgreSQL expresses it as `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE`, MySQL as `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, and the SQL standard as `MERGE`. It is safer than the naive pattern of SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE because that pattern has a race condition: between the SELECT and the write, another transaction can insert the same key, causing either a duplicate-key error or a lost update. The UPSERT performs the check-and-write as one indivisible operation protected by the unique constraint, so concurrency cannot slip in between.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India keeps a daily-balance row per account. The naive way is: check if today's row exists; if not, insert it; if yes, update it. Under load two requests can both check at the same time, both see "no row," and both try to insert — one crashes with a duplicate key. An UPSERT is like telling the clerk "create today's row, or if it already exists just update it" in one breath, so two simultaneous requests cannot both think they are the first.

**One line to remember:** An UPSERT inserts-or-updates in one atomic statement; it beats SELECT-then-write because the latter races between the check and the write.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive insert-or-update is three steps in the application: SELECT to see whether the key exists, then branch to INSERT if absent or UPDATE if present. Under concurrency this is a classic check-then-act race. Two transactions both SELECT and both see the key missing. Both attempt INSERT. One succeeds; the other violates the unique constraint and fails, or in a worse design overwrites and loses the first write. You can paper over it with retries, but that is fragile.

An UPSERT collapses the check and the write into one atomic statement that the database executes under the protection of a unique or primary-key constraint. In PostgreSQL, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key_columns) DO UPDATE SET ... tries the insert; if it would violate the named constraint, it instead runs the update, and inside the update you can reference the proposed row with the special EXCLUDED alias. You can also write ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to simply skip conflicts. In MySQL, INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE does the same, referencing the new values with VALUES() or the newer aliased form. The SQL-standard MERGE matches a target against a source and runs WHEN MATCHED or WHEN NOT MATCHED branches.

The safety comes from atomicity plus the constraint. The engine takes the appropriate row or index lock so that only one of the competing statements wins the insert and the other is routed into the update branch, rather than failing. There is no window between a separate read and write for another session to interfere.

The senior nuances: ON CONFLICT requires an actual unique or exclusion constraint to conflict against — it cannot resolve on an arbitrary WHERE. Under high contention an UPSERT can still deadlock or wait on row locks, so you keep the transaction short and insert keys in a consistent order. And UPSERT interacts with auto-increment sequences: a conflicting insert may still have consumed a sequence value, producing gaps, which is normal.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India maintains one running daily-total row per account. Many transfers for the same account hit the service concurrently, each needing to create today's row or add to it.

Problem 1 — the naive check-then-act races. We show two concurrent requests both seeing "no row today" and both trying to insert, with one failing on the unique key.

Problem 2 — the UPSERT is atomic. We show INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE adding the amount to the existing row's total, so concurrent requests serialize correctly on the unique key with no duplicate error.

Problem 3 — the update can reference the proposed values. We use the EXCLUDED-style new value to add to the running total.

The code models a ConstraintStore with a unique key on (account_id, day), a naive path that can throw a duplicate-key error, and an upsert path that is safe, plus a demo running both.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE daily_totals (
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    day        DATE        NOT NULL,
    total      DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id, day)            -- the conflict target
);

-- PostgreSQL UPSERT: insert today's row or add to the existing total atomically
-- INSERT INTO daily_totals (account_id, day, total)
--   VALUES ('SAV2001', CURRENT_DATE, 50000)
--   ON CONFLICT (account_id, day)
--   DO UPDATE SET total = daily_totals.total + EXCLUDED.total;

-- MySQL equivalent:
-- INSERT INTO daily_totals (account_id, day, total) VALUES ('SAV2001', CURDATE(), 50000)
--   ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE total = total + VALUES(total);
```


sections.s5_journey:
Input: four concurrent threads each adding Rs.50,000 to SAV2001's daily total for 2026-10-25, run once with the naive path and once with UPSERT.

Step 1 — Naive path. All four threads start together. Each checks "does today's row exist?" and several see "no." More than one then attempts INSERT for the same key. The first wins; the others hit the duplicate-key violation and are logged as failures. This is the race condition exposed.

Step 2 — The naive path leaves the total incorrect and noisy with errors, because concurrent inserts collided instead of accumulating.

Step 3 — Safe UPSERT path. All four threads call the atomic upsert-add. The first creates the row with Rs.50,000; each subsequent call conflicts on the primary key and is routed into the update branch, adding its Rs.50,000 to the existing total. No duplicate error ever occurs.

Step 4 — The final total is a correct Rs.200,000 because all four contributions were serialized atomically on the unique key.

Final output:

```

2026-10-25 17:39:00 [INFO] INSERT SAV2001|2026-10-25 total=50000

2026-10-25 17:39:00 [SEVERE] naive path failed (duplicate key race)
2026-10-25 17:39:00 [SEVERE] naive path failed (duplicate key race)
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```

    │
    ├─ NAIVE check-then-act                 ├─ ATOMIC UPSERT
    │  SELECT exists? → several see "no"    │  INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (account,day)

    │  1 succeeds, 3 duplicate-key FAIL      │  1 inserts, 3 routed to UPDATE branch
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An UPSERT is a single atomic statement that inserts a row if it does not exist and updates it if it does. PostgreSQL writes it as INSERT with an ON CONFLICT clause that names the conflicting key and a DO UPDATE action, where the proposed new row is available under the EXCLUDED alias; MySQL writes it as INSERT with ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE; and the SQL standard offers MERGE with matched and not-matched branches. The whole point is that the check and the write happen as one indivisible operation protected by a unique or primary-key constraint.

It is safer than the naive pattern of SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE because that pattern contains a check-then-act race. Under concurrency, two transactions can both run the SELECT, both see the key missing, and both attempt the INSERT; one succeeds and the other either fails with a duplicate-key violation or, in a worse design, overwrites and loses the first write. The UPSERT removes that window entirely: the engine takes the right row or index lock so exactly one competing statement wins the insert and the others are cleanly routed into the update branch instead of failing.

In our National Bank of India system we keep one running daily-total row per account, and under load many transfers for the same account arrive at once. With the naive check-then-act path we saw duplicate-key errors and an incorrect total because concurrent inserts collided instead of accumulating. Switching to INSERT ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET total equals the existing total plus the excluded amount made every concurrent contribution serialize correctly on the primary key, so four simultaneous fifty-thousand-rupee adds produced exactly two hundred thousand with no errors. The caveats I keep in mind are that ON CONFLICT needs a real unique constraint to conflict against, that heavy contention can still cause waits so I keep the transaction short, and that a conflicting insert can still consume a sequence value and leave a harmless gap. The line I remember is that an UPSERT inserts-or-updates in one atomic statement, and it beats SELECT-then-write precisely because the separate read and write race under concurrency.
